reasoning: Both outputs satisfy all four stated expectations, so the decision turns on two things I verified by execution rather than reading. First, the dispositive check: B opens with `disable-model-invocation: true` as a named frontmatter key, gives a command to check it, explains the mechanism (the flag strips the description out of the model's reach, making any rewrite futile), and states that deleting one line is then the entire fix. This is not speculative — grep finds `disable-model-invocation` referenced in 190 SKILL.md files under ~/.claude/plugins on this machine, and it is the single most likely cause of the reported symptom. A names the concept only, buried in an assumptions-table row ('If it's user-invoked-only, no description on earth will fire it'), never names the key, never gives a check, and omits it from both its Step 0 four-point triage and its final checklist — then assumes 'Model-invoked' and proceeds. Second, command verification. Each output's method rests on one load-bearing harvest command that mines the user's transcripts for real prompt phrasings; every downstream step in both documents depends on its output. B's harvest works exactly as advertised: 2 seconds, 10 short verbatim typed prompts ('fix the metric first', 'this is my current portfolio in interactive. analyze it'). A's harvest exits 0 and prints plausible-looking results, but is materially wrong for its stated purpose. Its filter `select(.type=="user" and has("promptSource"))` — described as pulling 'one line per typed prompt' — matches only 1509 of 16709 user lines across ~/.claude/projects, and every one of those carries promptSource="sdk". Measured against the same keyword pattern, it returns 16 unique prompts where the unfiltered version returns 67 (76% dropped), and the 16 it keeps have a median length of 2424 characters: long machine-authored SDK/mission prompts, the opposite of the short typed phrasings A tells the user to harvest. It also takes 62 seconds. This is the more dangerous defect class, because it does not look broken — the user would paste SDK boilerplate into their description believing it was their own vocabulary. A's other broken check is its collision grep (`grep -rh '^name:' ~/.claude/skills ~/.claude/plugins | sort | uniq -d`), whose stated pass/fail rule is 'Any output is a collision'; it emits 194 lines on this machine, including agent definitions, README.md files, template placeholders (`name: "[PM Name]"`, `name: Skill Name`), and marketplaces/ mirrors of cache/. Under A's own rule the user stops at Step 0 and never reaches the rewrite. B is not clean either: two of its five commands fail. `ls ~/.claude/skills/ ~/.claude/plugins/*/skills/ | grep -i <skill-name>` aborts under zsh ('no matches found', exit 1, zero output) and returns nothing under bash, for a skill that exists four times on disk — exactly the silent-false-negative failure mode that matters here. Its §6 neighbour grep `grep -rh "^description:" ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md ~/.claude/plugins/*/skills/*/SKILL.md` returns 0 lines under zsh and 7 under bash against 311 SKILL.md files actually present, because plugin skills live at plugins/cache/<marketplace>/<pack>/<version>/<skill>/SKILL.md, not plugins/*/skills/*/. Both of B's failures are in auxiliary checks, and B's own `find ~/.claude -name SKILL.md -exec grep -l "^name: <skill-name>" {} \;` does the same discovery job correctly (verified: returned 4 correct paths), so the user has a working route to the same answer. B's accuracy is also independently corroborated: the three neighbour descriptions it quotes for ab-test-analysis, cohort-analysis and sql-queries are verbatim correct against the files on disk, which grounds both its 'house pattern' rewrite shape and its near-miss competition analysis in the user's real installed set. A's near-miss handling is hypothetical ('a SQL skill, a spreadsheet skill, or a charting skill'). A is genuinely strong and close: its Step 4 warning — never summarize the workflow in the description, because the description is in context and the body is not, so a procedural description produces a skill that fires and is then followed shallowly — is a real, non-obvious failure mode B lacks entirely, and A is the only one whose worked rewrite actually contains the negative boundary clause it recommends. Its closing checklist is the more usable artifact. But B additionally supplies the structural escape hatch A relegates to its stress test (§5: if you cannot name four distinct triggers, the skill's scope is the problem and no wording rescues it), a failure-shape triage table that maps each observed symptom to a distinct lever, and a sharper account of the user's literal complaint — that a maximally generic description matches specific prompts worst, which is why the misses cluster on the cases that mattered. B wins on the dispositive check, on the correctness of the one command everything else depends on, and on grounding its claims in the user's actual skill set.
